The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) yesterday or the day before asked whether the government would give consideration to amending the rules of the house to provide for the establishment of a standing committee on social security, health, housing md public welfare. The answer is this. The government will have to give careful consideration to the question as to whether it is advisable to increase the number of standing committees, at least for the present session. As the hon. member indicates in his question, an amendment to the rules of the house would be necessary for this purpose. The subjects which the proposed committee would deal with are all subjects which could probably be considered appropriately by the standing committee on industrial relations. 
The hon. member for Eglinton also asked me the other day when the report of the national housing administration would be made to parliament. I am informed by the officials of that administration that they expect to have the report completed and in a position to be tabled by the end of next week.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a
question of privilege. Citation 68 of Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, reads as follows:
If a member who has heard the question put does not vote, and the attention of the Speaker is directed to the fact, the latter will call upon him to declare on which side he votes; and his name will be recorded accordingly.
I understand that this citation can be invoked only at the time a vote is being taken, so I cannot now ask that anything be done about hon. members who refrained from voting last night. That is not my question of privilege. However, I do feel that if we as members of this house are to cooperate with Your Honour in insisting upon the observance of the rule that all hon. members in their places when the question is put should vote, I should call attention to the fact that a practice is developing which should be corrected.
The situation last evening was this. We realized that some pairing arrangements between government supporters and members of the official opposition had been made, but as far as those of us in this group were concerned we did not know what those arrangements were. When we noted certain hon. members to our right refraining from voting on the amendment to the amendment, we could only assume that they were paired. Later we discovered that this was not the case.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: They were paired.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
Oh, no; the pairs are not listed in Hansard. I refer to the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and the hon. mem-

House of Commons
ber for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), who did not vote on the amendment to the amendment and who, as far as the record shows, were not paired. Had I known at the time that they were not paired, I would have called Your Honour's attention to this citation and asked you to have them declare on which side they were voting. As I have said already, it seems to me that if we are to cooperate with Your Honour in insisting upon the observance of what I believe to be a very good rule, namely, that every member present should vote, you might direct the attention of the chief whips to the matter and suggest that either one of two things be done; that when pairing arrangements are made, all the whips be advised of those arrangements, or that any member who is sitting in the house and is paired should indicate that fact after the vote has been taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: On the point raised by my hon. friend, in the first place there is no such rule in this house. We discussed this matter very thoroughly in the committee that was appointed a year ago to look into certain amendments and changes to the rules of this house. This rule applies in some other parliaments, but it does not apply in this house. There was a far more flagrant breach of the rules of this house last evening, in that some hon. gentlemen came in and took their seats while the vote was being taken. In regard to pairs, parliament knows no pairs.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Yes, and we studied that point last year very thoroughly. In the light of all the precedents, usages, customs and conventions of this assembly for many years, it is not the rule of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
Show me where that
is so.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
Now that the question of voting has come up I think on a point of privilege I might refer to something which occurred last evening, so that hon. members will not think that in voting I broke a pair I had with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McCulloch). I was under the impression that this pair began to-day, and aceofd-ingly voted last evening. Apparently the hon. member for Pictou believed the pair began yesterday or the day before. If there has been any misunderstanding I rise simply to
say that it was inadvertent, and a mistake on my part. I thought it only fair to say this for the benefit of hon. members opposite, and also that the hon. member for Pictou might understand the circumstances.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: With all due deference to what the minister has said, Mr. Speaker, I should like your ruling on this point, because I quite understand that I was obeying the rules of this house last evening. We had an experience of this nature in the last parliament, and the Speaker of that day certainly indicated that a member was not forced to vote if he had not made up his mind as to which way he should cast his vote. For future reference I should like to have your ruling in the matter.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Before you give your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs if he recalls a time some years ago when this very question was brought up. I cannot give the date at the moment; I did not know this matter would be discussed or I should have looked it up. I remember very well, however, that a few of us in this corner were compelled to vote under this very rule. So, unless it has been changed, that certainly was the rule under the Speaker of that day.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Perhaps I may be allowed to say a word in order to keep the record clear. The hon. member who just spoke did not intimate to the house that on the occasion to which he refers the members who had not voted were named to the Speaker, wherfias last evening no one was named as not having voted.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
I would say to the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) that in England members are compelled by the rules to vote, but in this house there is no rule obliging a member to vote. In answer to the hon. members who have questioned the practice of pairing in the house, may I draw their attention to paragraph 95 at page 49 of Beauchesne, third edition, where we find this:
Although there is no standing order in this regard, either here or in the English parliament, it is customary in both places for a member who has to be absent to agree with another member that he also shall be absent at the same time. Thus these members are "paired" and a vote is neutralized on each side of the question.
There can be no parliamentary recognition of this practice (pairing), although it has never been expressly condemned; and it is therefore conducted privately by individual members, or arranged by the gentlemen known as the "whips" who are entrusted by their political parties with the office of collecting their respective forces on a division.
House of Commons

So I may say that pairing is not recognized officially by our House of Commons.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to complete the record: If a rule is not observed, it should be taken out of the book of rules. At paragraph 69, page 25 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, we find this:
Under ancient custom, refusal to vote was considered a serious parliamentary offence, but the practice was changed in 1906 by the British house adopting a standing order whereby a member is not obliged to vote. That standing order does not apply to the Canadian Commons. The practice has not been changed in Canada where every member who has heard the question put is bound to vote.
And as I understand it, if an hon. member calls your Honour's attention to the fact that a member has been in his seat and has not voted, he is bound to declare himself one way or the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member?-just to help him. Since the rule was published there has been a decision by a Speaker of this House of Commons to the contrary effect. I am sorry I have not the reference with me, but that is the fact.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Does that alter the rule?-because we have so many decisions. Sometimes decisions have to be made for the convenience of business in the house. It seems to me that if we have rules we should abide by them.' Indeed, it seems to me no Speaker's ruling should supersede a written rule under a standing order adopted by the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: These are just marginal comments; they are not binding rules. Only the words in the standing orders are binding.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: They are cited in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Then what value has a written citation? Can it be cited one day and have value, and cited the next day and have no value at all?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: It is done every day, in the courts.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: That being so, what value has a book of rules of this description? One can find something in one of these books of rules to meet almost any situation which may arise, and to support almost any decision.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: It is like the bible.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: May I suggest that perhaps this discussion might now come to an end? No doubt it was the purpose of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to make this move for the purpose of drawing special attention to the fact that-

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker will tell my hon. friend when he should speak and when he should not. While I am speaking I have the floor.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: We had the same experience last year.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext: Their purpose has been served, in that they have drawn the attention of the public to the fact that two of our number did not, for various reasons, record their votes last night. I suggest that now the discussion might end-if their purpose has been served.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
The interpretation
placed by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) upon what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is entirely incorrect. I discussed this matter with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and we thought we should have it settled, because some of our new members do not fully understand the rules. We had told them that hon. members were bound to vote, and we think the situation should be cleared up. This was not done to bring before the house what any two members did or did not do-as a matter of fact I wish my hon. friend had not been challenged to name them, because it was not done with that intention at all.

maintopic: DIVISIONS-MEMBERS PRESENT WHEN QUESTION PUT AND NOT VOTING  PAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question has always been somewhat confused in this House of Commons. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) spoke of an incident which occurred at a time when he was a member of the house. He has pointed out that on that occasion the matter was brought to the attention of the house and that the hon. member in question was requested to record his vote. A year ago when we were dealing with a revision of the rules this matter was considered carefully by hon. members of the committee. At that time they did not think they should make a recommendation to the house in this connection. The postion I always took when

Business Visits to Europe
I occupied the Speaker's chair was that an hon. member who was in the house should record his vote; but if he did not do so the Chair had no power to compel him to do so.
Then, with regard to pairs; as has been already stated, pairs are not recognized in our rules. It is customary, however, between parties, for the convenience both of the house and of its members, that arrangements be made with regard to pairs. But so far as the rules of the house are concerned there is nothing which makes provision for them- although they are recognized by custom in the house.

subtopic: FACILITIES FOR FOOD, LODGING AND LIMITED TRANSPORTATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FACILITIES FOR FOOD, LODGING AND LIMITED TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
May I ask the Acting Prime Minister whether he has an answer to the question I asked the Prime Minister yesterday in regard to business men of Canada travelling in Europe?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): Yes; I was waiting for an opportunity to answer it. The question submitted yesterday by the hon member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) appears on page 494 of Hansard. I should perhaps read it to make the answer pertinent. It is as follows:
A press dispatch from Paris appearing in the New York Times of yesterday quoted the American ambassador to France as saying that facilities for food, lodging and limited transportation for American business men will be provided through the United States Embassy over there on and after October 1, 1945. May I ask the Prime Minister what steps this government is taking to provide similar service to Canadians on business in France and anywhere in Europe where the army has quarters and messes?
This is the answer which has been prepared by the Department of External Affairs; we are informed that, as a result of discussions which took place some time ago between the state department and the war department, the United States military authorities had been requested to cooperate with the embassy in Paris in working out arrangements for accommodating and assisting United States business men on visits to France. The details of the arrangements were to be worked out in the field between the embassy and the military authorities. Such arrangements as are reported in the press would be in line with the proposals.
Canadian offices in liberated countries have given every assistance to Canadian business men and others who travel to those areas and will continue to do so. As the house is fully aware, food, housing and travel facilities are extremely scarce in liberated territories. The army has been in close contact with the Canadian embassies in France and Belgium on this question and has provided facilities for
External Affairs

food and lodging whenever there were facilities available. These arrangements are being expanded.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): Yesterday a question was submitted to the Prime Minister, in his capacity of Secretary of State for External Affairs, by the bon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). It appears at page 491 of Hansard, and is as follows:
I do not think the answer given by the Prime Minister quite covers what I have in mind. 4 was wondering whether any representations had been made regarding the disposition of persons and property. The question I had particularly in mind was this: Is Canada interesting herself in the fate of many of the people who are moving around Europe at the present time, the disposition of whom will be discussed by the foreign ministers in London?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied:
I should like to have that question stand. I will give a further answer to-morrow.
The answer I have been asked to make on his behalf is: As stated yesterday in particular relation to the Yugoslav-Italian frontier, the Canadian government has not put forward any representations respecting European boundaries. The government is, however, very much concerned with the effect which the peace settlements will have on future relationships with the community of nations.
As regards displaced persons, Canada has taken an active and responsible part in UNRRA which is the organization charged by the united nations with coordinating the work of caring for and repatriating displaced persons. Canada is also represented on the executive committee of the intergovernmental committee on refugees whose main task will be the care and settlement of persons who will not be able to return to their homes.

subtopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Labour if he has any information to give to the house in regard to the progress made in the settlement of the Ford' Motor Company strike.

subtopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext:
I had notice of a question of a similar nature from the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), and as they both cut across the same thing perhaps I might deal with his question and the question of the hon. member for Vancouver East at the same time.
On Wednesday of this week I sent the following telegram to the president of the Ford Motor Company and to the president of Local 200, UA.W.-C.I.O.
Arthur J. Rheaume, Mayor Windsor, has wired Minister of Labour for Ontario as well as myself as follows: "Telegrams were forwarded to-day urging Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited and union to request intervention of yourself and provincial Minister of Labour in present dispute. Company reply not yet received but union has authorized me by letter to request that you and the provincial minister of labour set a date for a meeting with union and company representatives either at Ottawa, Toronto or Windsor preferably the last mentioned." I have consulted by telephone Minister of Labour Hon. C. Daley for Ontario who is at Kirkland Lake to-day and I hereby invite the president of the company and one other and the president of the union and one other to meet with the Minister of Labour for Ontario and his deputy and with myself and my deputy at Minister of Labour's office Toronto on a date which is acceptable to you both. Arrangements could be made for meeting on Monday October first if this is acceptable or any other day next week. The meeting would be under my chairmanship and purpose would be to discuss the work stoppage with a view of convassing the possibilities of bringing about resumption of work.
So far no reply has been received from the union to the invitation to meet with the representatives of the Ford Motor Company in the presence of the Minister of Labour for Ontario and myself, but I understand from press reports that the union is willing to participate in this meeting.
A telegram was received last night from the president of the Ford Motor Company, which reads as follows:
Your wire twenty-sixth instant received inviting representatives of company to meet yourself and deputy and Hon. Mr. Daley and deputy together with representatives of union. Since and including thirteenth instant union in addition to illegally picketing company's factory premises has by means of mass unlawful picketing forcibly prevented company's office employees official of company and all persons having business with company's office from entering company's main office premises in this city. You will appreciate that without records and office

Labour Conditions
facilities company's office work consequent upon cancellation of war contracts and with respect to reconversion as well as other important business matters which can be dealt with only in the main office is at a standstill. This unlawful deprivation by union of free and unobstructed ingress to and egress from the company's main office premises has been the subject of formal representation by the company to both municipal and provincial authorities but has now continued for fifteen consecutive days. Acceptance of your invitation in these circumstances would in the company's opinion constitute acquiescence in the unlawful action by the union and would invite similar tactics should future differences arise. Upon discontinuance of the above described mass unlawful picketing of main office premises the company and receipt of satisfactory assurance of no resumption thereof I am prepared to meet you in Toronto on October first or other day to be arranged accompanied by two other representatives of the company to discuss as suggested by you the work stoppage with a view of canvassing possibilities of bringing about resumption of work. If meeting arranged consider president of company and two other company representatives should participate and have no objection to equal number of union representatives acompanying union president.
W. R. Campbell, President Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited.
I should like to make this further observation with regard to the condition which the company lays down before attending the proposed meeting. I would say that the alleged illegal picketing is a matter governed by the provisions of the criminal code, responsibility for the enforcement of which lies with the provincial authorities. I understand that information has already been laid against one employee charged with illegal picketing, and court proceedings are pending. It would be improper, therefore, for me to make any comment at this stage. I have, however, conveyed to the officers of the union the contents of the com-* pany's communication.

speechtext: It is only fair that I should say that the question to which the minister referred when he rose was to have been asked by me on behalf of the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) who is unavoidably absent. It has been fully answered by the minister.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: EFFECT OF STRIKE OF MONTREAL LONGSHOREMEN ON PERISHABLE GOODS
speechtext:
I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, and his answer to one part of that question will perhaps be sufficient. During the day I have had an urgent long-distance telephone call from one of my constituents who is, perhaps, Canada's largest importer of Dutch bulb stock from Holland. In the Montreal harbour at the moment are two shipments of

Housing

$50,000 each awaiting transhipment from the Dutch steamer Boskoop. I see you are about to rise, Mr. Speaker, but I assure you I shall establish at once the urgency of the question. The cargo, as I say, is now awaiting transhipment to the Canada Steamship Lines, but the longshoremen have not been working for some days. These goods are of the most perishable nature and there is great urgency about the question which I am going to ask. First of all, have the longshoremen gone back to work, and secondly, if not, what steps does the government propose to take with respect to perishable goods of this kind, which will not stand any lengthy delay in transhipment to other boats?

maintopic: EFFECT OF STRIKE OF MONTREAL LONGSHOREMEN ON PERISHABLE GOODS
speechtext: I may observe, by way of preface to my remarks, that it has been said this was a strike against meat rationing on the part of the longshoremen. I am assured by the officers of that organization that it was a strike against the people who were striking against meat rationing. That may seem peculiar, and I see that my hon. friends are smiling, but you cannot load ships on salads. You have to have solid food. The longshoremen themselves need meat to do the heavy work they have to do. However, I am glad to be able to assure my hon. friend that the strike is over. The first gangs went to work this morning, and we expect the port to be in full operation by to-morrow morning.

speechtext:
I was waiting for an opportunity
to answer it. I regret that I was not in the house when the question was asked. The hon. member's query was as follows:
Will the minister kindly inform the house whether immediate steps can be taken to release building materials to discharged soldiers in order to enable them to build or remodel houses or places of business for themselves and their families?
Building materials are released automatically when a building permit is obtained. The government has no machinery for release of materials other than through the issuance of building permits, although they can be bought, of course, through the retail establishments
[Mr. Graydon.)
in any locality. Permits are given freely for small houses, and usually for alterations of houses. With regard to larger houses the need is carefully assessed in order that available materials may be directed to the smaller type of houses.
As far as shops are concerned, it is not possible at this time to release materials either for building new shops or for remodelling existing ones. We feel that we must get the housing situation in hand before we can extend the territory for -which, building materials can be released. However, the material situation is improving greatly. It is wholly a matter of manpower. We are still short manpower in the production of foundry products, electrical and other trades, and we are very short indeed of construction labour for the work on the site. The situation, as I say, is improving, and I am hopeful that later this autumn we shall be able to release permits for the remodelling and perhaps the building of shops.

^PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF $1,365,000,000 FOR WAR PURPOSES, DEMOBILIZATION, PROMOTION OF TRADE AND INDUSTRY, ETC.
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, inter alia,
1.	That sums not exceeding $1,365,060,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1946, for-
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	the expeditious demobilization of the Canadian armed forces;

War and Demobilization
(d)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and
(e)	the carrying out of any measure deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the war.
2.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. 1931, such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $1,365,000,000 as may be required for the purpose of defraying such expenses or making such advances or loans, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
3.	That the governor in council be empowered to reexpend, advance or loan moneys that may be received by way of refund or repayment of advances, loans or expenditure under the War Appropriation Acts of 1939 (second session), 1940, 1941, 1942, 1943, 1944 and 1945.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe that you, sir, and the house are already familiar with the general purpose and nature of this resolution as a result of the consideration of the previous resolution and bill last week, which provided for immediate use a portion of the funds asked for under this resolution.
The form of this resolution is almost identical with those which have been introduced in previous years, asking for authority to introduce a bill designed to provide the appropriation required for war expenditures. There is a difference, however, which hon. members will no doubt have noted, in the detail of the resolution, which is that item (c) of paragraph 1 is a new item, providing explicitly that the funds being appropriated may be used "for the expeditious demobilization of the Canadian armed forces". This specific reference to demobilization will be carried over into the bill, both by the inclusion of the clause mentioned and by appropriate references in the title and preamble. This shift in emphasis to include demobilization is similar to that which took place after the last war in 1919, when parliament passed the Demobilization Appropriation Act. In view of the substantial number and amount of continuing costs of the war other than demobilization proper, I think it is more correct at this time to entitle our bill "The War Expenditure and Demobilization Appropriation Act".
I think it is essential at the beginning to realize that war expenditures proper must continue for some time after the actual end of hostilities. We have still very large bills 47696-35J
to pay for the actual costs of equipping and supplying our fighting forces, particularly in the case of the army. Our forces are still mobilized and in many cases still beyond Canada, and they must be provided not only with pay and allowances, but with food, shelter, clothing and various other supplies and services. Some of our forces are engaged in the occupation of enemy territory and costs will continue to be incurred on this account for some time. The process of demobilization and discharge of the forces itself involves heavy expenditures apart from those of gratuities and re-establishment credits. The sudden termination of our war production involves very heavy expenditures in reimbursing contractors for costs which they had already incurred for production that will not now be needed and for other costs of cancelling war contracts. Many of the other more indirect costs of the war must continue, at least for a brief period after the end of hostilities-for example, the cost of the subsidies which are necessary in order to maintain our stabilization policy against the serious threats of inflation arising from shortages created by the war. Many outstanding accounts between Canada and Allied countries, particularly the United Kingdom and the United States have still to be determined in detail and settled.
It is clear, therefore, that quite apart from any future operations, however fast we manage to return to peace-time conditions and however strictly we may limit the incurring of new costs, the government will be faced for some months with heavy expenditures arising from the war. It is, of course, the government's earnest desire, as I am sure it is the desire of all members on both sides of the house, that war expenditures shall be terminated now as soon as possible. I should also state that it is our hope, and I am sure it will be the hope of the house, to return as quickly as possible to the normal peace-time practice of presenting detailed estimates to parliament to be voted in detail, rather than total appropriations to be voted as a whole, which practice has been and is still necessary in war appropriations, where so many uncertain amounts and unforeseen contingencies must be anticipated.
The amount of the appropriation for which the government is now asking is $1,365,000,000. Adding this to the interim appropriation of
War and Demobilization

$2,000,000,000 provided for war purposes by the last parliament in April of this year, we obtain a total for the fiscal year of $3,365,000,000. This total may be compared with total war expenditures for other years, but in doing so it is necessary to include in other years the amounts requested for Mutual Aid and similar purposes, because this year Mutual Aid was included as one of the purposes for which the interim appropriation could be used. It will be noted that this amount of $3,365,000,000 is $1,085,000,000 less than the total of the war and the mutual aid appropriations provided last year. Thus it represents already a very substantial reduction in our war expenditures, despite the fact that it contains very large amounts of bills carried over from previous years and large costs for the termination of war production. Moreover, it will be noted that the amount required for the latter half of this year is very much less than that required for the first half, even though many of the expenditures to be made in the latter half were really incurred during the period of fighting.
Before proceeding to speak of the estimates on which our total appropriation is based, and to note some of the factors affecting such estimates, I wish to emphasize that there is still a great deal of difficulty in forecasting our expenditures accurately, and therefore in making firm estimates even now when the fighting is over and when half the fiscal year is finished. In many cases, of course, our estimating problems are easier because we no longer have to make highly uncertain assumptions about the course of military operations and the amounts of equipment and supplies that will be necessary for them. The remaining new costs to be incurred are largely those connected with personnel, and once the programme of demobilization has been reasonably well established, we can expect to forecast with some accuracy costs of pay and allowances, travelling, transportation, and similar items. On the other hand, a great many of the costs which will be seen in the detailed estimates of the services represent amounts still to be paid in respect of equipment, services and supplies obtained some time ago. In many cases substantial amounts have already been paid by the Department of Munitions and Supply for these items, but the final bills have not yet been presented to and paid by the service departments. In the relatively short time since the termination of hostilities, it has not been possible to calculate with accuracy how much one should therefore allow in the estimates for refunds to the

Department of Munitions and Supply accounts, which should be deducted from the total amount required by the government as a whole. In other cases, supplies have been obtained from the United Kingdom and the United States and some payments made on account, but there remains a balance to pay which it is difficult to forecast until final decisions are reached in regard to the details of amounts and prices. Finally, there is the cost of the termination of war contracts, arising from the sudden end of hostilities last month. There has not been time in the last few weeks fully to assess the effect of that happy event upon the costs of war production. Immediately upon receiving word that Japan was prepared to surrender, the government proceeded to cancel thousands of contracts for the production of munitions and other supplies, and, of course, our chief concern was to see that these cancellations were made , as promptly and economically as possible. After this has been done, much work is still needed to determine exactly what the costs on all this multitude of accounts wTill be, and I must confess that in framing our estimates for the amounts required for cancellation of contracts we have had to proceed on the basis of informed judgment of those in the best position to know, rather than on a detailed analysis of accounts which cannot be completed quickly enough for our purpose.
I have stressed these points about outstanding accounts because I believe it is vital for the house to realize, first, that many of the costs still to be paid are in- respect of operations now completed, and, secondly, that there is still considerable uncertainty as to exactly what these will turn out to be.
For the convenience of members of the house in the debate on this appropriation, I propose to place on Hansard, if I have the unanimous consent of the house, tables showing the various estimates for departments, which have been prepared and considered by the government in arriving at the figure for the appropriation for which parliament is being asked. War and Demobilization
Hon. members will note that the amount which the army estimates it will require for the current fiscal year is approximately SI,068 million, which compares with an estimate of $1,535 million for last year and actual expenditures for last year of $1,244 million. I should point out that it has always been particularly difficult to forecast the army's requirements accurately because it has drawn the bulk of the supplies it has currently required from United Kingdom stocks and paid for them as they were used. Consequently its expenditures depended very much upon the actual course of operations, and it was necessary to leave a considerable margin of safety in such items as ammunition, armament, and fighting vehicles. On the other hand, this year the army in particular is faced with a large accumulation of outstanding accounts to be settled for items supplied to it in previous years both from Canadian and United Kingdom sources. This will be quite evident to members if they examine with care the items for the additional amounts required in the balance of the fiscal year in the various categories under army services, where considerable amounts are shown for items of which obviously no substantial future deliveries will now be necessary. Of course, the principal questions of substance in regard to the expenditures which the army will be incurring henceforward are the rates of demobilization and repatriation, and the size and nature of the occupation forces and the continuing army establishment. These are matters which must be left for the Minister of National Defence to explain and to discuss with the house, and I shall therefore not attempt to make any comment upon them except to say that on financial grounds, as well as other equally important grounds, the government has been determined to see that nothing is allowed to stand in the way of the most rapid and most equitable repatriation and demobilization of our forces.
For naval services the amount of the estimate for the current year is approximately $300 million, which compares with an estimate last year of $410 million, and actual expenditures last year of $417 million. It will be noted from an examination of the details in the case of the navy that there are still substantial amounts to pay on outstanding accounts for equipment, ammunition, armaments, vessels and supplies of one sort and another which were obtained during the course of hostilities. The fairly rapid pace of demobilization in the naval services is indicated by the fact that pay and allowances for the last seven months of the year, that is, the additional amounts required
for this category, are only about half what they are for the first five months, despite the fact that special factors like clothing allowances and extra leave upon discharge swell the costs of this item.
In the case of air services, the estimate requested, after allowing for recoverable items, is approximately $600 million compared with an estimate last year of $1,090 million and actual expenditures last year of approximately $1,260 million. It will be noted in the case of air services that expenditures for the latter part of the year are substantially below those for the first five months. When one examines the details, the reason for this becomes evident as it shows up in the practical disappearance of the cost of maintenance of overseas squadrons. This is possible because the air force does not have now such large outstanding accounts as the other services have for supplies already received. The reason for this is that the cost of the overseas squadrons is paid monthly and there are not the same outstanding problems in determining the rate of such payments as there are in the case of the army.
I think it is unnecessary for me to make any particular comment on the items for sundry services under the Department of National Defence, which have been estimated for the current year at approximately $17 million as compared with $22 million last year. I should point out, however, that for administrative reasons the responsibility for military relief was transferred to the Mutual Aid board from the Department of National Defence, and consequently the expenditures on, and estimates for, this item no longer appear among the sundry national defence services, as I indicated they would in April of this year. Now that I have made reference to this item, I may well go on to point out that expenditures on it last year are shown at a total of $50 million, and the estimates of the amount required this year are shown to be $34 million, all of which have already been allotted. These expenditures represent the cost of supplies procured in Canada and shipped overseas for distribution by the combined military authorities during the course of military operations and in the zones of military control. They represent a part of the cost of military operations which takes the form of the provision of supplies to civilian populations on whom the military are dependent for assistance and co-operation or for whose maintenance they are responsible during the time they are in control of the territory. The countries receiving such supplies
