have been requested to pay for them, and it is expected that a large part of the moneys expended in this way will be recoverable.
It will be noted that the estimate for the Department of Munitions and Supply for the current year is $282 million, as compared with an estimate of $183 million last year and actual expenditures last year of approximately $216 million. These figures all exclude the effects of the amount recoverable from munitions production allotment fund and allotted to other expenditures outside the department which is shown separately at the bottom of the summary table. The nature of the expenditures for which this estimate is requested has largely changed from previous years, as now the main item is $175 million to cover the costs arising from the termination of contracts. These termination or cancellation costs are to be covered by one large item in this way rather than by individual items under the various headings appropriate to the use for which the deliveries were intended had the war gone on. Broadly speaking, this item therefore represents the cost of terminating our war production suddenly as a result of the unexpectedly early end of the hostilities against Japan. I should add that this figure does not represent the total cost, as there is also likely to be necessary some writing off of amounts advanced for production out of the munitions production allotment fund. As I have already warned the house, however, any estimate of these termination costs at this time is only an informed guess and it will be some months before we can be sure whether the figure included here is too high or too low.
The costs of Mutual Aid this year have been met from the interim war appropriation passed by parliament in April, as was specifically authorized in that appropriation, as well as from some funds carried over from the earlier Mutual Aid appropriations. Mutual Aid requirements were particularly heavy during the first five months of this current year-indeed, right up until the end of hostilities. Shipments of munitions and other war supplies to allied countries were at a high level in the opening months of the year while hostilities were still proceeding in Europe. After victory in Europe, the need for munitions and military supplies fell off substantially, but a good deal of war production was still required, particularly of aircraft and naval vessels for the war in the Pacific. On the other hand, there was a very drastic decline in the expenditures overseas of the Canadian army and air force, which had been providing the United Kingdom with Canadian dollars to pay for the cost of war supplies
'Mr, Ilsley.]
required from Canada. Consequently the need for Mutual Aid on the part of Britain remained at a high level during the period of intensive preparation for large scale operations in the Pacific.
In the figures of requirements for the current year for Mutual Aid, I have separated those for UNRRA, which will continue, from those for allied countries to which transfers of supplies as Mutual Aid were terminated as of September 2. The total allotted to Mutual Aid from the interim appropriation was $720,224,000. The amount required to complete our first contribution to UNRRA, in addition to the expenditures last year, is $65,907,000, all of which will. I expect, be spent this year. Deducting this from the total allotment leaves $654,317,000 as the amount required for Mutual Aid to allied countries from this year's appropriation. This figure includes the estimated cost of production of certain items not delivered by September 1, but which will be completed in the expectation that they can be sold. The proceeds of such sales cannot yet be estimated, but they will in due course be credited to our Mutual Aid account.
It will be noted that I have included a figure of $25,000,000 for UNRRA in the further amounts required for the current year but not yet provided. This is intended to enable us to furnish, before the end of our fiscal year, a portion of a second contribution to UNRRA, which the Canadian government has agreed' to make, provided that the United States and other contributing nations will also make a second contribution. The total of our second contribution would be the same as our first, that is, one per cent of our estimated national income for the year ended June 20, 1943, which amounts to $77,000,000 in all. It would mainly take the form of contributions of Canadian supplies, but it may be that we will contribute- a portion- in cash, as we did the first time, to provide UNRRA itself with some funds to meet expenses in Canada and elsewhere. I might add that in fact UNRRA is spending a large amount of its own free funds in Canada, as practically the whole of our first contribution was committed for the purchase of Canadian supplies at a fairly early date this year. I feel sure that all Canadians will be gratified that Canada is able to furnish substantial amounts of urgently needed supplies to the poor and suffering people of Allied countries through this democratic, international organization. The house will, I understand, hear further about UNRRA, if it wishes, during the debate on the war appropriation-, and there will be an opportunity to discuss Canada's part in UNRRA.

War and Demobilization
The amount estimated to be required for the Department of Veterans Affairs is, of course, considerably higher than in previous years. It includes pension costs for the veterans of this war andl for various others who have been accorded' pension rights similar to the armed services such as merchant seamen, fishermen, civil defence workers, etc. It also includes costs of hospitalization and rehabilitation benefits for veterans. It does not, however, include the qpst of war service gra-tuites and reestablishment credits, which are payable by statute out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund. The amount which we estimate will be required for war service gratuities and reestablishment credits is approximately $240 million, which will, of course, be an expenditure in addition to the appropriation being requested under this resolution and in addition to the amounts specified in the main estimates which have been presented to the house.
It will be noted that only the relatively small amount of $5 million for reconstruction projects has been included in the estimated amounts required this year. This is intended to cover only the costs incurred before the end of March next in projects not directly provided for by other departments, such as public works or housing, and which may be required, it is believed, on a relatively small scale in a few localities to meet the danger of unemployment in those areas of persons who cannot reasonably be expected to move to other areas where work is available and to make a start on some urgent developmental projects. This is in accordance with the general policy explained to the house the other evening by the Minister of Reconstruction. As he explained, there is a large volume of private work ready to go forward as soon as materials and labour can be made available for it. Much of this private investment is necessary if Canadians are going to be able to have steady and remunerative jobs in industry. In addition, all available building materials and, I believe, building labour, are urgently needed now for the building of houses, and we do not wish to utilize our scarce building supplies for public projects that can be deferred until later, when the acute housing demands have been met. So far as one can tell at this time, it appears that total expenditures in Canada, private, public and for exports, will be sufficient to maintain employment as a whole at satisfactory levels, despite the rapid rate of demobilization and the termination of war production. There will obviously be problems in the movement of workers to take advantage of the new demands
which are taking the place of the war demands, which have now ceased. I do not myself believe that large expenditures on reconstruction projects will be needed in the next six months to facilitate this process of readjustment. The general policy and philosophy of the government in regard to public investment have, of course, been set forth at considerable length in the proposals made by the government to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, and I do not believe it is necessary for me to enter upon them here. What I do wish to point out is that the provision made in the present appropriation is based upon an appraisal of the situation over the next six months only, and cannot be taken as any guide to the scale of reconstruction expenditures that will later be required.
In conclusion I would like to say a word or two about the general scale and nature of our expenditures for the current year. Adding together the appropriations for war expenditures, the items covered in the main and supplementary estimates, and the items to which I have referred above for gratuities and re-establishment credits, one obtains a total of between $4,600 million and $4,700 million for expenditures in the current fiscal year. To this must be added certain other cash requirements, particularly those for export credits and the financing of the foreign exchange control board, which will bring our total requirements for the year above $5 billion. These are formidable figures. They show that the scale of our financial operations remains at the high levels achieved in the war. They make clear that the task of the Minister of Finance is still a difficult one. On the other hand, they mask to some extent the decline-the rapid decline -that is already occurring in the government's demands upon goods and services of the community. Already the government has cancelled practically all its contracts for purchases for war purposes. The substantial expenditures still to be made on these accounts represent almost entirely settlements in respect of past operations and the cancellation of contracts. At the same time, our armed forces are being demobilized as rapidy as is reasonably possible in all the circumstances. Indeed, I believe that this month the total number of men being released exceeds an average of 2,000 a day. The government is paying these men substantial amounts of deferred pay, of pay for leave upon discharge and clothing allowances, and will continue payments to them for some months in the form of gratuities and reestablishment credits. These men will nevertheless be available for useful employment in other fields. Even our expenditures under the main estimates this year
War and Demobilization

include a much higher proportion than normal of what we may term "transfer payments," which do not represent a demand on the part of the government for either goods or services. This applies to the very large figures both for family allowances and for interest on the public debt, which, taken together, constitute well over half of the total of these estimates.
Bearing these facts in mind. I think it is evident that despite the apparently large totals of government expenditure this fiscal year, the activities of the government are in fact being rapidly curtailed, and supplies and services are being released quickly for use in meeting the demands of Canadian enterprise and Canadian consumers.
I should like before concluding to say a word or two about the scale of our expenditures and other cash requirements in relation to the ninth victory loan. This loan is to be obtained in the latter part of next month and the early part of November. It is to be our greatest victory loan, the climax of the series of outstanding successes which have been achieved in this vital part of our war finance. We have already announced that the minimum objective for the loan is to be one and one-half billion dollars-the largest objective we have ever set. It is natural that many people should be surprised that we should need so much money now that the fighting is all over, and I want to make the reason clear.
In the first place it should be realized that this is really two loans in one-it is intended to cover our borrowing needs for a year, and not for half a year, as previous victory loans have done. This is possible because our expenditures are declining rapidly and we believe we can now get along with one loan- if it is a big one. Our last two victory loans have each produced about a billion and a half dollars, which in each case has met our needs for about half a year. This new loan, which we hope and expect will exceed its objective and yield well over one and one-half billion, is intended to cover our needs for a full year. There will be no victory loan or similar loan next spring.
During the year following this ninth victory loan, and for which it is expected to provide the moneys required over and above our revenues, our expenditures and other cash requirements, including the loans we propose to make to allied nations for reconstruction, will probably amount in all to about four billion dollars. About thirty per cent of this will be for the normal and continuing expenses of civil government. The balance will include the costs of demobilization and rehabilitation of our servicemen, the costs of bringing them 
home from overseas, the costs of our occupation forces and post-war military forces, part of the cost of terminating war production, and some costs for reconstruction and new postwar development. It will also include hundreds of millions-how many I cannot yet say-for loans to allied nations for supplies urgently needed from Canada during the period of reconstruction. The government intends to ask authority from parliament in this session to make sqch loans to allied countries on a large scale.
In view of these large requirements I believe wTe must borrow something approaching two billion dollars for this period. This is a huge amount, even though it is much less than the totals we have borrowed in recent years. Something on this scale is required, however, if the total reduction in our expenditures and cash requirements is not to be reflected solely in our borrowing. It is with these needs in mind that we established one and one-half billion as the minimum objective for the ninth victory loan. I hope and believe that we will be able to exceed this objective by a good margin and thereby obtain from this one loan nearly all the borrowed money we shall require to carry us through until the fall of next year.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I am sure that the house has
listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister has had to say. It is not my intention to speak at this time. I had intended to speak for half an hour or more, and will take the opportunity of doing so later. For the information of the house I may say that one of our members, who is very much concerned with the war appropriation measure, has to leave, and I am therefore giving the floor to him. I refer to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green).
Before he rises to speak I should like to say a word or two with respect to one item mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), namely, the forthcoming victory loan. Plans for the securing of that loan is the task of the government, but I wish te say to the house at this time that we shall be glad to lend our support to the successful flotation of that loan. With these brief remarks I give the floor to the hon. member for Vancouver South because what I have to say can be said at a later time.

Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to my leader fot giving me this opportunity to speak, and to the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell), who also agreed that I should go ahead.

War and Demobilization
I propose to say a few words about our defence forces and something about the policy that will be adopted with regard to them. I had intended to make my suggestions when the house is in committee, and I am a little premature in making them now on behalf of my party, but I am sure that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Gibson) will understand my reasons for doing so.
We are convinced that it would be in the interests of the house and of the country if the Minister of National Defence would make some broad statement of government policy with regard to Canada's defence forces in the years that lie ahead, rather than making two statements, one for the navy and one for the army, with a third statement to come from the Minister of National Defence for Air. It will be very difficult for the hon. members to give proper consideration to the policy if it comes piecemeal, namely, if the navy policy comes first and then two or three days later the army policy, and finally two or three days after that the air force policy. We should like to know the general picture. It may be that the air force is to be greater, as compared with the other forces, than before the war, or the same may be true of the navy or the army. We should like to have the over-all picture at the opening of the debate if the government can arrange to give it to us.
It seems to me that at the present time the Canadian people are very uncertain as to what the defence policy of this nation should be; perhaps there is some uncertainty in the minds of the members of the house and of the ministry, because it is a very difficult problem to solve. But there are certain facts which should be kept in mind. The first is that our civilization has been saved by our efforts during the last war. That is something we should never overlook. We should also remember that for a whole year the British peoples-I mean the peoples of the different nations of the commonwealth and of the colonial empire-stood alone between our enemies and the destruction of civilization. None of the peoples of the empire have any reason to hang their heads over the part they have played during the war. And of course that is true of Canada. Our fighting power was used to great advantage and was a real factor in winning the war. Our production of supplies and equipment has been splendid, and we have every reason to be proud of the part we have played.
Now Canada and the other nations of the world who believe in freedom are determined that there shall be no more wars; but rather than take the attitude which was taken after
the last war by saying, "Now let us forget all about war; there wiE never be war again," we are determined to defend the peace by force if necessary. I think that is the attitude of every nation that believes in freedom. Canada must play her part in defending the peace. There are other factors, too, which nust be kept in mind. There have been extensive scientific developments. I need only mention radar, rocket projectiles and the atomic bomb, which is made primarily from uranium from the pitchblende found in our own Northwest Territories. That fact alone should give Canadians a good deal of concern over our future defence policy. As I say, there have been, tremendous scientific developments during the period of the war. Another fact is that Canada is now more vulnerable than ever before. I certainly hope this may not be, but I think we must bear in mind that with aU these developments Canada might be the battleground if there should be another war.
Having those facts in mind, various members of the official opposition have given consideration to certain broad principles which we believe can be approved by everyone in this house and which we think will help the Canadian people to crystallize an opinion as to what the defence policy of Canada should be. In the first place we believe that two obligations in regard to defence should be recognized by the house and the Canadian people. The first is that we must be prepared to defend Canada to the very best of our ability. The second is that we must remain in a position to live up to our commitments to the united nations organization. This means that we must be prepared to do our share, by force if necessary, to maintain world peace. We must not get into the frame of mind where we expect somebody else, somebody else's sons, to be responsible for our defence and for maintaining world peace.
That is the first broad principle. The second is that we must not destroy the efficiency of our fighting forces. We on this side of the house are very much concerned for fear that is happening at the present moment. There is a great movement to demobilize, which is a perfectly proper thing t>o do; but we have met with this situation. Young officers have come in to us. For example, I had a young officer of the navy, with a distinguished career, come to me and say, "I should like to carry on in the Canadian navy. I think it is a grand profession; I think there is a service to be rendered to Canada and to the world, and I -should like to stay on. But I cannot find out w'hat the conditions are to be. I do not know what the rates of pay or the pensions are to
War and Demobilization

be; or how many men will be required; as a result I have made up my mind to get out of the navy and go back into business." We had a young battalion commander, twice decorated for gallantry, one of the outstanding soldiers from my province of British Columbia, come in and say the same thing. He wanted to stay in the Canadian army, but he could not find out anything definite and he was not prepared to wait for a two-year period and take a chance on being able then to get back into business. So he decided' to get out just as quickly as he could. We have had the same position taken by outstanding men in the air force, and I think it is also true of skilled men in the ranks of all the services. I quite realize the government's difficulty. I know it is frightfully hard to draw up a definite policy at this stage. But there is a time element which enters into the picture, and the human factor must also be considered. Perhaps the better the man is the more determined he will be to get out if he does not have any reasonable assurance that he can make a career in the armed forces of Canada. We all know what happened after the last war, during which the Canadian corps had a record second to none; we were all intensely proud to belong to that corps, and the same was true of the air force and the navy; yet after the war very little attempt, was made to maintain efficiency.
-Now here we are again with very efficient forces, none better in the world. Let us adopt a policy that will enable us to maintain efficiency even while we have to cut down the size of the services. I do not think we can afford to delay. The same thing is true with regard to equipment and supplies. Let us remain in a position to be able to manufacture, as much as possible, whatever equipment is needed for our forces. We did very well in that regard during the war; let us make sure we can continue to carry on in the same way. If we do not take these steps and trouble does come again, the price of our failure and neglect will be paid with the lives of our sons. They are the men who will have to pay the shot if this house does not adopt a proper policy at this time. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, in advocating efficiency I am not advocating waste. We intend to check very carefully for any waste that may be found in the appropriations, but we believe that efficiency must be the main consideration, certainly during the period which lies immediately ahead, while everything is up in the air and no one can tell what the world situation will be.
Our third broad principle is that the defence forces must be given the help of our scientists. Every facility must be afforded to the defence

forces to enable them to keep up to date and to get the most modern improvements, not only in the way of equipment but also in the way of training. During last winter or perhaps early in the spring arctic and sub-arctic exercises were carried out in western Canada by the Canadian army. I believe one exercise was conducted in northern Saskatchewan and one in British Columbia. In the latter province it took place between the main lines of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National but still it was a sub-arctic exercise. I believe those should be extended; that the forces should be able to carry on further exercises of that type. They should be able to carry on exercises in the Northwest Territories up toward the arctic, up above where these pitchblende deposits are located, and in the Mackenzie river district. They certainly will never be able to do that if the attitude of the house and of the Canadian people is to be the same as it was after the last war. The carrying out of exercises such as I suggest would help open up that northern country. I believe that in due course several hundreds of thousands of people can be settled in northern Canada, and that there can be a great development in that area. This has happened in Siberia, where the Russians have had outstanding success; and there is no reason why in our country Canadians cannot do the same; if the army and the air force working together could carry out exercises of that type it would be a great help in opening up that northern country. There are many other things that could be done if we had efficient forces properly supported by the House of Commons and by the people of Canada.
The fourth broad principle is that there should be the closest coordination in training and in types of equipment among the different nations of the empire, and also with the United States. This must always be borne in mind. A good example of the success of this type of venture is to be found in the British commonwealth air training plan. We cannot stand alone; we must work with other people, and I think the natural thing for us to do is to coordinate our efforts with those of other British peoples and of the people of the United States.
These are the four broad principles we suggest. We believe in them; we are convinced that they are at least worthy of the most careful consideration of the house and the people of Canada. In connection with their consideration, and for the benefit of the defence forces of Canada, we believe it would be helpful if there were set up a standing committee of this house on defence matters.

War and Demobilization
In the United States house of representatives there is a committee on naval affairs and one on military affairs; I believe that they have similar committees in the senate. We see no reason why we could not have committees of that type in Canada; in such circumstances we would be in a position to call chiefs of staff before such committees, and to find out their reasons for doing certain things and for wishing to have certain plans adopted. In this way, too, we would get the members of the House of Commons and the Canadian people more solidly behind the defence forces. In these modern times the defence of a country involves every man, woman and child. It is no longer a matter of a few trained men; everybody is vitally interested. I am sure great help would come from civilian members who happened to serve on committees of that kind. We ask for support of this suggestion from the various parties in the house.
That is all I have to propose to-day. I repeat the hope that everybody will support us in our submissions. We think the defence of Canada, the constitution, the training anc the work to be done by her fighting forces should be above politics, and something to which we should all agree.
May I repeat the request I made when opening, that the Minister of National Defence try to give us an over-all picture when he makes his statement, which probably will not now be made until the first of next week.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has placed before us a most comprehensive outline of the proposed expenditures for the coming year for war purposes and demobilization. It was a lengthy and detailed statement which, of course, will be discussed more thoroughly when the house goes into committee.
May I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member who has just spoken. I believe he placed his views before the house in a clear manner, and in a non-partisan spirit which should be appreciated by all of us. In his observations he raised some questions and made some suggestions which are worthy of more than passing consideration.
It seems to me that when we are discussing these estimates on this occasion we should consider them in a manner very much along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), namely, in the light of the policies we are likely to follow in the next few years. I agree with him that those policies cannot immediately take shape in a concrete form. But at least when we are discussing the problems arising out of defence
and demobilization I suggest we should keep in mind the kind of external policy Canada will have to follow in the next few years.
It was that phase of the problem I had intended to discuss this afternoon, because obviously one has had no time to consider the very much detailed and comprehensive financial report which has been placed before the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I should like to say, as the hon. member for Vancouver South implied, that the situation to-day psychologically is vastly different from the situation which we all faced at the end of the first world war. At the end of that war I think many were filled with the idea that perhaps we had seen the last of all the great wars, that we were about to organize some form of collective security which would ensure universal peace for a long time. There was a very high idealism-a Christian pacifism, if you will-which permeated the minds of most men and women of good will in every part of the world and in every party. But in the last ten years there has been disillusionment.
Not all countries were thinking of peace.
I believe there has been disillusionment in the last ten years, and I am speaking of what might be called Christian countries, and men and women of good will.
Germany was not.

I am not including Germany, because no one could include that country as a country having Christian ideals from the rise of Hitler in 1933 to the present. But I believe it is true to say there was that feeling throughout the democratic world. I regret very much to say that to-day to a large degree that feeling is absent; and to a considerable degree I believe that absence can be traced to a feeling of uncertainty with respect to the future. Even those of us who had the privilege of attending the great conference at San Francisco realized while we were there that there were great dangers in the international situation. There were tremendous difficulties to iron out, and we realized that we had to consider the future defence of our various countries and of peace itself very realistically indeed.
Whether we have witnessed, as some of us did, the flying bombs going over London a year ago, or whether we have only read about them and seen pictures in the moving-picture theatres, and whether we have only read of the atomic bomb, I believe we have learned another lesson and know perfectly well to-day
War and Demobilization

that any form of isolation must be entirely removed from our minds. Isolation is not a policy any more-if it ever was. We are all vulnerable to attack from without, in the event of another war. We have to hope and trust and pray that the nations of the world, realizing the danger that besets them, will not again turn to the dreadful arbitrament of war, if I may put it in that way. We have to face the future realistically and do all that must be done for the defence of our own country and our own civilization.
When we have approved the united nations charter we may be in a better position to see what Canada should really do, but until that is done we must consider the defence problems of this country from the point of view of this country and of the allied nations with which this country has cooperated throughout the entire war. I was hoping that by this time the nations of the world would have adopted the united nations charter and that perhaps some of its provisions might be operative now, particularly in so far as the security system was concerned. Under the security council there will be established a military staff representing the general staffs of the five principal powers. That military staff will be obligated to enter into agreements with the various nations that adhere to the charter. Hence we should get some idea of the part that Canada should play in the world security situation. We do not know that at the present time, and consequently we have to gear our policy to what this house, this gov-ernnment and this country believe to be in their interests at the present time. I do not know when the military staff of the united nations will be established, and I do not know when Canada will be called upon to enter into some agreement for the general security of the world.
This is what I really had in mind when I rose to speak this afternoon. In all probability this was the last of what we might call the traditional wars, wars in which great armies moved and men fought in close combat. The rocket bomb and the application of atomic energy to bombs have provided a new phase of warfare and one of which we must take cognizance at the present time.
The hon. member for Vancouver South spoke a few moments ago of the necessity of maintaining our scientific and industrial strength. It is altogether probable that scientific research and industrial strength may be of greater import in the future than our armies. In looking over these estimates I was surprised and sorry to see that there has been no increase in the appropriation for the national research council. Indeed there is a slight de-

crease in the total amounts in the war appropriation bill and the civil estimates. I think that is wrong. I think any one who knows anything about Canada's part in the development of radar and the development of at least the raw material for the atomic bomb realizes that the young scientists of this country played a very important role in the course of the war. We should see to it that we do not lose these young scientists because, while they may not be our first line of defence, they will be at least our second line of defence in the event of another war. I find that the estimates, civil and war, for the national research council have been decreased from some $5,000,000 to just over $4,500,000, that is taking the two estimates together.
Under the united nations charter raw material and scientific research may be regarded as one of our principal contributions to the world organization. As those who have read the charter will remember, the military general staff will negotiate agreements, not only with regard to the military aid, naval, army and air, which a nation will give, but will decide what that nation should do, in agreement of course with the nation itself, to assist in the enforcement of international decisions or the maintenance of security. We should look very carefully into this phase of the matter in considering the estimates now before us.
As the hon. member for Vancouver South has indicated, when we are considering these estimates we should make a careful study and report of the post-war military organization that this country requires and can best maintain. In other words, I think the country should know from the Minister of National Defence, indeed from all the ministers if you wish, the policy that Canada is to pursue in organization, the allotment of personnel among the three forces and, as I have said already, in the realm of scientific research, industrial training, war-time mobilization and so on.
Let us bear in mind that at the end of the last war there was a disposition on the part of military leaders to think of future wars in the terms of the war that had just ended. That was a very natural disposition, and I do not think there is any profession or trade represented in this house that might not be guilty of the same kind of thinking. We think rather in terms of what we have been doing than in terms of changes in the manner of doing what we should do. I am not singling out the military profession in this particular. In my opinion in the period which will follow this war there may be a danger that methods which are becoming or

War and Demobilization
have become obsolete since August 6 may be the methods which the military leaders of this and other countries may wish to follow.
We remember how France emerged from the last war with probably the most powerful army in the world and then continued to train that army largely-not wholly of course -on the assumption that- the war which might come again would be like the war in which France had been victorious with her allies in the period 1914-18. The result was that the more progressive military leaders like de Gaulle, who wished to change the tactics of the French army, were not paid any attention. We know what the result was in 1940, when the French army crumbled before an army which had been organized on a new basis with new and different equipment. Consequently I think the house should bear in mind that there is a disposition on the part of any profession to keep its policies in line with what it has known in the past, and we should exercise care lest we allow that to happen again in our country. We must beware that we do not merely allow the desires and the prerogatives of those who have served us well in high places in the army, navy and air force to dominate our thinking and our programme, because they may again be thinking, not in terms perhaps of personal advantage, but in military terms that are becoming obsolete.
One other fact I should like to mention at this time is this. In dealing with demobilization we have to think of the men who are to-day overseas. We have, for example, large forces in Holland which are being gradually reduced, and Holland to-day is very largely under military government. Perhaps when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) goes to Holland he may find that there is considerable criticism by our Dutch allies of the military government we have established in Holland. I have been told by young men who have just come back from Holland that there is a good deal of discontent with our arrangements there. For example, the Dutch people find that, while they have no transportation, our own military transportation is quite adequate not only for our needs but if used to meet the needs of the population, but there are regulations which do not permit our military in Holland to assist in the transportation of supplies or even the refugee people who are found along the highways. That may be a matter of military necessity, but some young men who have recently returned from Holland fail to understand the situation, and have told me that it is causing a good deal of misgiving among the Dutch and is upsetting some of the splendid relations which exist
there. Those of us who were in Belgium and France a year ago-I think it is a year ago to-morrow that we went across to Belgium- will never forget the enthusiasm with which the people of Belgium and France met our car with the Canadian maple leaf painted on it as one of the symbols, and the friendliness with which our boys were greeted everywhere. It would be too bad if we lost that very fine and friendly spirit in the low countries.
The hon. member for Vancouver South suggested that a defence committee of this house be established where matters of defence could be discussed and members would become more thoroughly acquainted with what was necessary and with the policies which were being followed, and could interest the people of the country. I think that is a good idea, but I was going to suggest something a little different. I intended to suggest that we try to establish a non-partisan committee, which would be a mixed committee of civilians and military men, to go continuously into the field of defence. That is not unlike the suggestion which has already been made. Somewhere at least we can find a suitable committee to deal continuously with these matters. That would be helpful. Before the recent war we had too little discussion in this house, and certainly too little discussion before any committees of the house, regarding the necessities with which the country was then faced. That I think was particularly true after Munich. May I remind the house that Munich was hailed by most of the people of this country as a great step toward universal peace. It was at that time that I was jolted into believing that war was coming, but we in this house did not give the attention to the policies behind the naval, military and air force estimates which I think should have been given, nor did we give attention to the external policies which were likely to make military arrangements necessary. I am therefore very glad indeed that the government has seen fit to grant the request which has been made from time to time in this house over the years and to set up a special standing committee to deal with external affairs. In that way the house should be well informed as to what the necessities of the external scene will demand.
I do not think I wish to say very much more this afternoon, but I wanted to bring these points before the house and the minister in the general discussion before we go into details. In the light of the present world situation we cannot neglect them. The united nations charter will be discussed in this house. I do not propose to anticipate that discussion, except to say that I believe there is not a thinking man who reads and understands the
War and Demobilization

dispatches which are coming from Europe, and indeed from all over the world, who does not believe deep down in his heart that the international situation has deteriorated since the united nations charter was adopted at San Francisco. I think when we were there we felt that there was reason to hope that the great powers would understand each other a little better and that the longer the conference continued the better that understanding would become. It looked that way. Watching the news to-day, and reading all that comes to us through the press and in articles from well-informed sources, one is forced to the conclusion that the world is in a desperate condition.
So, then, I say to the minister that we shall go into these estimates with a great deal of sympathy; we shall endeavour to find out what they all mean, and we shall bring before him observations which may sometimes appear, perhaps, to show a very critical spirit. But I assure him and the house generally that in doing so we shall have only one end in view, namely, to make our contribution as a nation to the establishment throughout the world of universal law, order and peace.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River):	Mr. Speaker, I shall not take very much of the time of the house just now to deal in any detail with the estimates which were placed before us a short time ago; but I thought I should say a few words, particularly in response to the suggestions which were made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). I felt that the hon. member very skilfully placed before this house a number of principles to which every dynamic Canadian could subscribe.
I feel and have always felt that Canada must be strong, not only in a naval, military, and air force way. These strengths are necessary, to be sure, and we have always in this corner of the house advocated that Canada should be prepared. We have never lost sight of that necessity, and if hon. members will look back over records of sessions during the last ten years they will note that we have been consistent in advocating a strong and a prepared Canada.
We need to be strong economically also, because faith in Canada of a dynamic kind cannot be engendered into our people unless we have ensured the well-being of every family in Canada. That is important, and I would suggest to the government that, while they are making their plans and laying their policies for the years to come, economic strength be given the most earnest and careful consideration along with preparedness in a military way.
I have felt for some years that Canada 	.
perhaps has been trying to do too much considering the population that we have had. We need more people in this country. We have a grand country, which is capable of maintaining, I would say, a population of fifty million people, and we cannot be strong and virile until such time as we have increased our population to the extent that it is possible for us to stand forth as one of the first-rate nations of the world in the way of population as well as in strength of natural resources. I do not know whether the government has given any consideration to means by which, during the next few years, the population can be successfully increased. I will not take the time of the house to advocate any particular principle. Perhaps the government have already laid their plans. It may be necessary for us to combine several methods of accomplishing this objective, but surely there is one thing certain, that the population will not increase sufficiently by natural means-through the birthrate-unless and until we remove from our people fear of want. That is the thing which accounts in the main for small families, and I say to you, what is the use of having a strong navy, a strong army and a strong air force to save the country for posterity if there is not going to be any posterity?
We must realize, Mr. Speaker, that methods of war to which we have been accustomed in the past are outmoded; and because those methods are outmoded we must revise our ideas of war. We must revise our ideas of defence, and, I might add, our ideas of security1-world security as well as Canadian security. I have heard to-day things which lead me to believe that we have not changed our ideas one particle since before the atomic bomb became a reality. My judgment is that we are up against something in that regard where we have no human experience to draw upon, and therefore we need a new approach, a complete revision of our ideas on security. I hope that this Parliament in the next few weeks will prove itself capable of meeting the new conditions and of revising its ideas so as to be thoroughly prepared for the exigencies of the future.
W'hile we are making Canada strong, we must at the same time be prepared to contribute of our strength to ensure the preservation of Britain. Britain is in danger. Britain is in a serious condition. If Great Britain is destroyed the British commonwealth of nations cannot endure; therefore we must be prepared to contribute of our strength to ensure that Britain will remain strong and virile, and that the British commonwealth of nations will be maintained. For I say to you, Mr. SEPTEMBER 28, 1945

Speaker, with all the gravity at my command, that the one great barrier in this world to-day against world domination by totalitarianism is the British commonwealth of nations. We must not allow ourselves to be lulled into a sense of false security and into the type of psychology that seemed to prevail among great numbers of the people of the country from 1930 to 1939. We were ostriches, in the main; *we hid our heads in the sand so that we would not see what was going on around us.
Manj- brave words have been spoken since we have learned world facts by experience, and tragic experience at that. Restless and warlike nations will hesitate to attack a strong, virile and well-prepared Canada. Let us therefore keep her in ever-growing strength.
One other thing we should not overlook as we face these, estimates, and study and discuss them in the days to come. An important source of strength, it seems to me, in any people, is to keep those people properly informed. A nation that is ignorant of the facts and the truth of the world situation, a nation that is victimized by the worst and most subtle propaganda imaginable, can never have that source of strength to draw upon which was mentioned so often in the old days: "Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free."
Along with all these other suggestions that have been given, the government ought to take note: of the need for watching, the sources of dissemination of information in this country, and see to it that the information that is fed to the people is the truth and not subversive propaganda. A strong people can stand the truth and they wilt react well to it, but if they do not. have the truth, the lack of it immediately becomes a source of disintegrating strength. Therefore I say it is necessary for us to keep in mind the importance of getting to our people information so that they can prepare themselves individually and so that they will not be victims of deteriorating propaganda. I say that whatever money is needed to accomplish the worthy objective of making Canada strong in every way, we in this house ought to be prepared to furnish, and without question. The group in this section of the house is prepared to go into the study of these estimates sympathetically and carefully, and to assist the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsltey) to accomplish for Canada the position which I have envisioned1 in my own mind, and which I am sure that every worth-while Canadian has envisioned in his mind.
Listening to the hon. member for Vancouver South, I was happy to hear the suggestions he made. I am sure that the group in this section of the house are prepared to accept
those principles as a working basis for the examination of these particular estimates, and we shall be prepared to extend to the minister every cooperation and help in accomplishing all worth-while objectives.

I rise only for the purpose of placing before the government certain questions with regard to the very important matter that must be determined, namely, is this country still at war? When will the proclamation be made that will terminate war in so far as the powers of the War Measures Act are concerned? Having regard to the proposals that have been brought before the house to-day, it seems apparent that the government of this nation intends to continue the fiction that the war is still proceeding, and will not terminate before March 31, 1946, at least.
But before asking these questions, may I as one who had the very humble position of an observer for the Progressive Conservative party at San Francisco say, after listening to-day to the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) and the speech of the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low)-which party throughout the years has represented no changed policy but has always realized the need of maintaining the British commonwealth of nations as the great instrument for peace and welfare in the world- that their speeches indicate that growing out of San Francisco has come a new feeling among the members of the house in their attitude and relationship to discussions on foreign affairs. Let me say that no greater contribution was made to a united front on the part of the Canadian people than when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) chose to send to San Francisco a non-political delegation representing various parties in the house. Only one error was made. That error was that there was no representative of the Social Credit party at San Francisco, a party which has long espoused such high principles in so far as the empire is concerned.
I came back from San Francisco believing implicitly that the fear of war, both actual and economic, had more or less passed into the realm of history. I heard those great men there; I felt their attitude. I know what the attitude of the Canadian delegation was. Let me say that that delegation did honour to Canada in the contribution they made at San Francisco. I thought I knew the attitude of those other men who represented the different countries of the world. But, sir, when the atomic bomb fell on Japan on August 8 there was an end to an era of man's thinking on international affairs, and I believe an end to man's thinking on life as it had been; for
War and Demobilization

now all realize more than ever as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said this afternoon, isolationism no longer can be the cult or the belief of any political party or of any nation. Therefore I believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) should give serious consideration to an increase in the amount that will be expended by. the national research council during the next year; because the atomic bomb not only has great dimensions of peril, but also has great dimensions in the improvement of living conditions and in the raising of economic standards everywhere in the world.
Coming from Saskatchewan I am very proud of the fact that a number of young scientists from that province have contributed to the work of the national research council and that prominent leadership was given to Canada by Dean MacKenzie of the university of Saskatchewan. These scientists now have the opportunity, with the knowledge that has been secured in the production of the atomic bomb, to improve conditions in Canada and elsewhere. Certainly, if we were able to spend billions of dollars for war, we should not be niggardly and spend only four and half million dollars in peace for the work of the council so that this council will be able to continue their work on the principles of atomic power to the end that our living standards may be materially improved in the days to come.
Would the hon. member permit a question at this stage? Before he finishes his fine address would he mind defining to the house just what he conceives to be the meaning of "isolationism"?

It would take a long time to endeavour to define "isolationism." It represents to me, sir, a state of mind, a psychological reaction, a failure to realize what conditions are in the world. Those are the things that develop isolationism; those are the things that permit nations and individuals not to have full appreciation of what is going on in the world. That is why it is so important at this session of parliament that we do not permit ourselves to be lulled into a false sense of security by reason of what took place at the San Francisco conference, and thereby fail to assure that Canada's defence within this empire shall be properly preserved in the future; for if we wait for a year, two years, three years or five years, the impetus and the experience of this war will disappear and dissipate, and we may again return to that isolationism which characterized so many in the days before the war.

I am not going into the details of the resolution, but 1 should like to secure from the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) at this time an answer to certain questions. These questions were outlined some days ago by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), at which time the Minister of Justice answered rather indefinitely that these matters-and I deduce this from his words- and their decisions had grave implications. I think the Canadian people have a right to know these things. They have a right to know whether this government intends to endeavour to carry on in the months ahead under the provisions of the War Measures Act. I am going to read only one or two sections of that act, but those sections indicate that, in fact, the resolution now before the house is in part founded upon the government view that the War Measures Act is still in effect. The resolution provides:
That sums not exceeding $1,365,000,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1946, for-
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada.
Those words "the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada" apparently are abstracted from the War Measures Act. Let me read section 2 of that act, which provides:
The issue of a proclamation by His Majesty, or under the authority of the governor in council shall be conclusive evidence that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists. .	. until by the issue of a further
proclamation it is declared that the war, invasion or insurrection no longer exists.
Section 3 gives the governor in council certain powers. Such things may be done by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war. To-day there is no real or apprehended war, in the opinion of the Canadian Bar Association, with which I think any reasonable person would agree. The section contains these words:
. . . by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion, or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada. . . .
Those are the identical words of the resolution. After referring in the preceding sections to the powers which may be exercised by the governor in council in consequence of there being any real or threatened war or insurrection, section 6 goes on to say:
The provisions of the three sections last preceding shall only be in force during war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended.

War and Demobilization
Does the government suggest that to-day we are in the midst of war? Does the minister suggest that it can continue th operation of the War Measures Act until such time, one year, two years, or three years or more hence, when they may by proclamation declare the war over? This is a matter of grave importance to the people of this country. Are powers being exercised by the government to-day which are beyond the compet nee of the government to carry into effect? The Canadian Bar Association, of which in recent years the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) was the distinguished president, has reviewed this matter at length. It was first discussed in August of last year, and in the report of the association this appears:
... it would appear proper to insist on having immediately after the hostilities have ceased, a proclamation of the governor in council, to declare that the state of war has ended.
That is the considered opinion of a body which I am sure the Minister of Justice must concede understands the situation with respect to that act. It takes this view because it believes that no longer should laws be enacted by regulation or order in council but directly by parliament; by the freely chosen representatives of the people in parliament instead of by controllers and others in similar positions. Coming down to 1945, the Canadian Bar Association made this declaration:
Your committee is of opinion that the state of war cannot and should not, even by the authority of a statute, be deemed to continue to exist when the war itself is over. Let us make the distinction here between the war emergency itself which is the fact of a state of war, and an economic emergency which, though a consequence following the war, is not the war emergency itself.
Therefore at this time I ask the Minister of Justice to enlighten this house and the country by answering certain questions which I believe are fair and reasonable. The first, to which I have already referred, is this:	Is
Canada still at war? In that regard, and to the determination of that question, I further ask the minister whether the law officers of the crown have given an opinion on that question. Has it been submitted to them, and what is the nature of the opinion they have given? The next question I wish to ask is this, in the words of the council of the Canadian Bar Association. Is it the intention of the government to continue from month to month to postpone the proclamation of peace in order to continue in effect artificial controls which, while excusable in war where necessary, have no place in a peace-time economy? The next question I ask is this. Are the defence of Canada regulations still in effect? In reading over the expenditures to
be made this year, I find that further expenditures are anticipated in connection with the administration of the defence of Canada regulations between now and the end of March, 1946.
These are matters, sir, which are of vital interest. As far as Great Britain was concerned, after the first war and again in May of this year she endeavoured at the earliest possible moment after the end of war in Europe to put a stop to anything bordering on undemocratic controls and the exercise of legislative power by controllers or by the government operating under order in council. She brought into effect an act extending the life of the emergency powers act; and in the old act of 1920 it was provided that His Majesty might declare that a state of emergency continued to exist:
... of such a nature, and of so extensive a scale, as to be calculated, by interfering with the supply and distribution of food, water, fuel or light, or with the means of locomotion, to deprive the community or any essential portion of the community, of the essentials of life.
They extended certain powers, but they also provided that no such proclamation should be in effect for more than one month, unless it was forthwith communicated to parliament, and that for such purpose parliament should be called into session within five days. They also provided that any regulations passed after the end of hostilities should be laid before parliament and should not continue in force after the expiration of seven days from the time they were so laid, unless a resolution was passed by both houses. I suggest, sir, that if the government is going to endeavour to continue to issue orders in council, it should immediately give assurance to the people of. Canada that no orders will be passed while parliament is in session; that this array of 60,000 orders in council that we have had during the period of the war, and that are even to-day being issued while parliament is in session, should terminate; and that any orders in council passed should be passed only temporarily, and should be operative only temporarily unless accepted by parliament.
I mention in this connection that while parliament is sitting, and when the war is over in Europe and in Asia, the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board to-day in Vancouver told the people of Canada what is to happen in Canada for the next year. This is what he advised as to what is to take place-and when parliament is sitting:
'	1. Canadians can expect controls on textiles
to continue at least until the end of the year.
2.	Strict rationing of sugar is indicated for at least another eighteen months, perhaps longer.

In other words, we in parliament find in the newspapers what the minister fails to place before us while parliament is in session. Then, next:
World shortages of food may dictate the "establishment or continuation of rationing and distribution controls well through the transition period".
Here we are in parliament, and this statement is made to the press.
The hon. member for Broadview endeavoured to get an answer to this question: Is the War Measures Act still in effect and are we still at war? And yet, while parliament sits on this 28th day of September, members ascertain from boards what the intention of the government is for the future.
And then, finally:
So long as price controls remain, the board expects to hold the line on the 1941 price levels, upon which ceilings are based.
Those, sir, are the statements made by the distinguished head of the wartime prices and trade board, made before parliament has found out anything about it, and made while parliament was still in session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the statements about rationing were obviously nothing more or less than statements about world shortages. You would have to ration, if you have world shortages-and that is all those statements amounted to. Then, the statement about holding the line at 1941 price levels has been made before, and made on behalf of the government and by members of the government.

They have not been made by any member of the government since the end of hostilities. The government made its statements of policy in this house as to what the wartime prices and trade board and other control boards would do while the war was on. And yet to-day, after being in this house for a considerable period of time, we are still expected to get information of this kind outside of parliament from a board responsible only indirectly to parliament. I am sure the Minister of Finance does not agree that there should be any declaration of future policy of this country by any controller or any head of a board while parliament is in session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board was simply stating what the board would be doing, within the principles of government policy as already stated. The hon. member may think that rationing of sugar, for example, would have to be stated as a separate policy. But the rationing policy just follows inevitably if there is a bad shortage of sugar. tMr. Diefenbaker.]

That does not follow inevitably. The board makes decisions under government policy; and that board has no power to pass orders in council in order to continue the policy, unless the War Measures Act is still in effect. That is why I wish to have an answer to that question.

Bring the matter before parliament.
